Constant CAR states and the periodic core

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Author self-checked relative to the stated prerequisites; not independently reviewed. New original text: public domain (CC0).

An infinite sequence of identical two-level density matrices gives a type III factor when the two eigenvalues differ. To find its parameter, we must compute a modular invariant. A period of one modular action, or even its complete group of inner times, does not by itself justify the subtype.

We use Infinite tensor products and their reference states, especially its explicit faithful product representation, local slice maps and closed modular graph, and Fermions, Fock space and quasi-free factors, including its direct constant-state type III proof in Section 20. Sections 4–5 below construct the represented period-circle crossed product and continuous core. Scalar Lebesgue integration and Hilbert completion underlie the Fourier and measurable-phase arguments.

The modular foundations can be followed through BG1–6, which prove normalization, fullification and the complete closed modular graphs for an arbitrary left Hilbert algebra. FC1–5 prove fixed-corner GNS and modular restriction for every faithful normal semifinite weight, even when the corner has infinite weight. These arguments supply the pure Hilbert-algebra and fixed-corner steps in the MG comparison. The finite-ideal graph closedness and every-weight comparison retain their stated prerequisite proofs. Type III corner transport is a separate prerequisite of the general reverse inclusion in MG-4; the product-spectrum upper bound below does not use it.

For the subtype inference, Section 6 uses the full finite-ideal spectral comparison and the every-weight fixed-corner comparison in MG-0–3. PP00–PP04 provide the concrete filter and factor-contact arguments showing that every integer modular degree survives in every nonzero fixed corner. We also compute the entire spectrum of the product modular operator from its coefficient domain. These two calculations determine the intersection over all faithful normal semifinite weights, including weights of infinite total mass. The center calculation then gives, for this factor with least positive center period LLL,

M is type IIIe−L.(1)M\text{ is type }\mathrm{III}_{e^{-L}}. \tag{1}M is type IIIe−L​.(1)

Here (1) is a consequence of the all-weight calculation, not a premise inferred from periodicity. The upper bound on the intersection comes from the explicit product modular operator; its lower bound comes from comparison with every weight. The general type III corner-transport step of MG-4 is therefore unnecessary for this particular upper bound. Its full stated proof remains available for the general comparison problem.

The periodic subtype calculation fixes a separable one-particle Hilbert space. The subtype calculation below assumes this space is infinite-dimensional. The earlier CAR lesson separately retains finite-dimensional and arbitrary directed finite-mode approximation statements.

Bernoulli measure and finite-permutation invariance

The following construction explains the measure and approximation steps used in Lemma 3.1. The domain is the countable product X={0,1}NX=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}X={0,1}N, with the identical Bernoulli probability measure in (10); the functions are complex elements of L∞(X,ν)L^\infty(X,\nu)L∞(X,ν), and invariance means equality modulo null sets under every permutation fixing all but finitely many coordinates. The conclusion is constancy almost everywhere. We retain 0<p<10<p<10<p<1, p≠12p\ne\tfrac12p=21​. The argument uses scalar measure and finite-coordinate independence directly.

We begin with ZFC with countable choice, completeness of the real and complex scalars, elementary finite sums/products and set operations, and the definitions of a sigma algebra, a measurable function and countable additivity. The construction proceeds from cylinders to the completed probability measure, scalar integration, L2L^2L2 approximation, and permutation invariance. The normal operator identification D≅L∞(X,ν)D\cong L^\infty(X,\nu)D≅L∞(X,ν) in the other portion of (10) is separate from this scalar function argument.

The first four subsections construct and complete the measure. Integration and cylinder density then justify the error estimate. Finite independence and the permutation action give the final constancy argument.

We prove the finite-cover property needed for countable additivity and outer measure, rather than invoking compactness. Suppose A∈AA\in\mathcal AA∈A is covered by a family of sets from A\mathcal AA but no finite subfamily covers it. Choose a head level expressing AAA as finitely many prefix cells. One of these cells has no finite subcover; otherwise the finitely many finite subcovers combine. Split that cell into its two children. Again one child has no finite subcover. Recursion gives nested prefix cells of lengths tending to infinity, each with no finite subcover. Their compatible digits define a single x∈Ax\in Ax∈A. Some member BBB of the given cover contains xxx. Since BBB is a union of cells at one finite level, the prefix cell of xxx at every sufficiently large level is contained in BBB. A cell in the recursive family is then covered by this one member, a contradiction. This proves the finite-cover property for every such cover of AAA.

The human comparison and the operator boundary

Sourav Chatterjee's Stats 310A (Math 230A) Lecture notes, Theorem 6.5.1 and its full proof on printed pages 60–61/PDF pages 64–65, give a real-valued invariant-function theorem using displacement of finite coordinate sets. Corollary 6.5.4 and its proof on printed page 62/PDF page 66 specialize it to finite permutations, the Hewitt–Savage zero-one law. The cited file is an undated 115-page author-hosted PDF.

The human proof invokes Exercises 5.1.3 and 5.1.4 for finite-coordinate approximation and representation; its final real threshold inference is brief. Those source exercises are not premises here. The construction from finite weights through cylinder density and completeness gives the full product construction, completion, scalar integral and approximation at the binary scope. The independence and permutation arguments, followed by Lemma 3.1, give complex finite independence, the completed almost-everywhere permutation action, and the full complex conclusion. The human theorem serves as a comparison of methods; every measure prerequisite used in this proof has been proved above.

We retain 0<p<10<p<10<p<1, p≠12p\ne\tfrac12p=21​. Some function arguments extend further, but no endpoint, half-state or nonidentical-product conclusion is asserted here. Countability is used in the cylinder algebra, countable covers, completed representatives and finite permutation group. Infinitely many coordinates are needed to move supports away from a given finite approximation, so no finite-product ergodicity claim follows.

Equation (10) has two distinct parts: the Bernoulli probability and scalar function space constructed above, and the normal identification of the multiplication algebra with the occupation diagonal DDD. The latter is not a premise of Lemma 3.1. Equality of cylinder moments alone does not close that identification. An application to DDD can use the separate operator argument or a complete normal identification; the scalar proof above uses neither as a substitute for its function statement.

All measure, integration, density and permutation prerequisites used in Lemma 3.1 are supplied at the stated scalar set-theoretic boundary. General products with arbitrary alphabets or index sets, normal multiplication-algebra or CAR transport, operator factoriality and type, subtype, crossed products, core and flow require their own arguments.

The measure and function-space construction now supports the proof of Lemma 3.1 by averages of disjoint coordinate copies.

Diffuseness and the finite-factor alternative

The diffuseness calculation can likewise be carried out with projections. Put q=max⁡(p,1−p)<1q=\max(p,1-p)<1q=max(p,1−p)<1. Every minimal diagonal projection in DnD_nDn​ has state value at most qnq^nqn. If a nonzero projection eee were minimal in DDD, the finite diagonal partition would decompose it into projections under eee; exactly one piece would be nonzero and would equal eee. Hence ϕ(e)≤qn\phi(e)\le q^nϕ(e)≤qn for every nnn, contradicting faithfulness. Thus DDD has no minimal projection.

The trace assertion before Lemma 3.1 follows from finite densities and Lemma 2.1. Bounded strong* convergence of both factors implies strong convergence of their products: for example,

∥(xnyn−xy)ξ∥≤∥xn∥ ∥(yn−y)ξ∥+∥(xn−x)yξ∥.\|(x_ny_n-xy)\xi\| \le\|x_n\|\,\|(y_n-y)\xi\|+\|(x_n-x)y\xi\|.∥(xn​yn​−xy)ξ∥≤∥xn​∥∥(yn​−y)ξ∥+∥(xn​−x)yξ∥.

Apply this to xn=En(x)x_n=E_n(x)xn​=En​(x), yn=En(y)y_n=E_n(y)yn​=En​(y) in the finite fixed algebras, and evaluate at Ω\OmegaΩ. It passes the finite trace identity to NNN. An isometry v∈Nv\in Nv∈N then has ϕ(1−vv∗)=0\phi(1-vv^*)=0ϕ(1−vv∗)=0, so vv∗=1vv^*=1vv∗=1; thus NNN is finite.

The finite-factor alternative used below has the concrete proof supplied in Section 8. If eee is a minimal projection, positive-part calculus shows that every selfadjoint element of eNeeNeeNe is scalar: two distinct spectral levels would give a proper nonzero projection under eee. Thus eNe=CeeNe=\mathbb CeeNe=Ce. Factor contact gives a nonzero element from eee to any nonzero remaining projection; its polar decomposition copies eee into that remainder. Each such orthogonal copy has the same positive trace ϕ(e)\phi(e)ϕ(e). The bound kϕ(e)≤1k\phi(e)\le1kϕ(e)≤1 forces a largest finite family, whose sum is one, since a nonzero remainder would admit another copy. The associated partial isometries give full matrix units. Each matrix corner is one-dimensional because eNeeNeeNe is scalar, so they span NNN. This proves that a finite factor with a minimal projection is a finite matrix algebra. An abelian subalgebra of a finite-dimensional matrix algebra has minimal projections, contradicting diffuseness of DDD. The comparison in Anantharaman and Popa, Proposition 2.4.13 and Corollary 2.4.14, printed pp.39–40/PDF pp.45–46, agrees with this alternative; its statement is not substituted for the projection proof in Section 8.

Multiplying (19) by 1⊗z−t/P1\otimes z^{-t/P}1⊗z−t/P puts u(t)⊗1u(t)\otimes1u(t)⊗1 in CCC. The coefficient operators π(x)⊗1\pi(x)\otimes1π(x)⊗1 are there too. They generate B⊗1B\otimes1B⊗1. Together with the central multiplication algebra they generate the right side of (21), proving the reverse inclusion.

For the center, take every second-leg vector slice of a central XXX. Each lies in BBB and commutes with BBB, so Theorem 4.2 makes it scalar. Compression by a fixed unit first-leg vector produces d∈L∞(T)d\in L^\infty(\mathbb T)d∈L∞(T) recovering each of these scalars. All second-leg slices of X−1⊗dX-1\otimes dX−1⊗d vanish, and their separating matrix coefficients give X=1⊗dX=1\otimes dX=1⊗d. Conversely every 1⊗d1\otimes d1⊗d is central. This is the full slice argument above at the represented tensor-product scope. □\square□

The modular foundations, finite-ideal closedness and balanced-weight corner comparison remain the explicit supplied prerequisites; their full proofs are the linked arguments, not an implicit classification input.

The source comparison is exact. Connes, Une classification des facteurs de type III, Section 2.2, printed pp.174–177, defines the full fixed-corner intersection and proves its factorial-fixed-algebra and equivalence properties. The two support witnesses above instantiate Proposition 2.2.2(c), whose proof is on pp.174–175. Theorem 3.2.1 and Lemma 3.2.2, printed pp.190–191, retain all faithful normal semifinite weights and the full GNS-filter passage; Corollary 3.2.7(a), printed p.192, agrees with the equality of S(M)S(M)S(M) and the modular spectrum when the centralizer is a factor. The present route uses the supplied balanced-weight and whole-graph proofs for its every-weight comparison, and the explicit coefficient resolvent for its upper bound. It does not import the source's general action-realization theorem or claim that its uninspected prerequisites have been proved here. The type notation is the discrete closed spectrum described in the introduction to Part IV, printed p.213. The original free primary paper supports this comparison.

Theorem 6.1. For a separable infinite-dimensional one-particle space and 0<p<10<p<10<p<1, p≠12p\ne\tfrac12p=21​, the constant-covariance CAR factor is AFD and of type

III min⁡(p,1−p)/max⁡(p,1−p).(28)\mathrm{III}_{\,\min(p,1-p)/\max(p,1-p)}. \tag{28}IIImin(p,1−p)/max(p,1−p)​.(28)

Proof. The completed CAR-to-product GNS identification transports the factor, the faithful state and the full modular graph. The central expectation argument in Section 1 proves factoriality, and Lemma 2.1 proves sequential AFD approximation. The tail-commutator and finite-projection contradiction proves type III. The preceding all-weight calculation proves S(M)={0}∪λZS(M)=\{0\}\cup\lambda^{\mathbb Z}S(M)={0}∪λZ, which gives type IIIλ\mathrm{III}_\lambdaIIIλ​. Independently, Theorems 3.2–5.1 and (24)–(27) give the center action and L=∣log⁡λ∣L=|\log\lambda|L=∣logλ∣. Thus the same parameter also satisfies (1):

e−L=e−∣log⁡λ∣=λ=min⁡(p,1−p)max⁡(p,1−p).e^{-L}=e^{-|\log\lambda|}=\lambda =\frac{\min(p,1-p)}{\max(p,1-p)}.e−L=e−∣logλ∣=λ=max(p,1−p)min(p,1−p)​.

For the source range 0<p<1/20<p<1/20<p<1/2, this is p/(1−p)p/(1-p)p/(1−p), the constant-covariance parameter. □\square□

The modular-action period is PPP, while the center-flow period is LLL:

P=2π∣log⁡λ∣,L=∣log⁡λ∣.(29)\begin{aligned} P&=\frac{2\pi}{|\log\lambda|},\\ L&=|\log\lambda|. \end{aligned} \tag{29}PL​=∣logλ∣2π​,=∣logλ∣.​(29)

For example, p=1/3p=1/3p=1/3 gives λ=1/2\lambda=1/2λ=1/2, P=2π/log⁡2P=2\pi/\log2P=2π/log2, and L=log⁡2L=\log2L=log2. Using e−Pe^{-P}e−P would give the wrong parameter.

At p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2, the state is tracial and the infinite factor is II1\mathrm{II}_1II1​. At p=0p=0p=0 or 111, the vacuum or filled Fock representation is irreducible and its von Neumann algebra is type I. For finite-dimensional one-particle space, every faithful constant state generates a finite matrix factor. None of these cases satisfies the hypotheses used in Theorem 6.1.

Exercise 5. Explain why identical mode densities are essential for the permutation proof. Then show that the centralizer is AFD without identifying its isomorphism class.

Solution. The tensor permutation unitary is fixed precisely when it commutes with the density. Identical densities give vπρ⊗nvπ∗=ρ⊗nv_\pi\rho^{\otimes n}v_\pi^*=\rho^{\otimes n}vπ​ρ⊗nvπ∗​=ρ⊗n, so the required permutations belong to NNN and preserve the state.

A two-leg swap already detects the issue for unequal parameters pj,pkp_j,p_kpj​,pk​. The occupation vectors 010101 and 101010, interchanged by the swap, have density eigenvalues

(1−pj)pk,pj(1−pk).(1-p_j)p_k,\qquad p_j(1-p_k).(1−pj​)pk​,pj​(1−pk​).

Their difference is pk−pjp_k-p_jpk​−pj​. If this is nonzero, the swap does not commute with the density and cannot serve as the fixed unitary in the permutation argument. The identical-density assumption supplies exactly the invariance and disjoint-support relocation used there.

For AFD, the fixed algebra in AnA_nAn​ is finite-dimensional. More explicitly, its density value on an occupation word of weight mmm is (1−p)n−mpm(1-p)^{n-m}p^m(1−p)n−mpm; these values are distinct for different mmm under p≠1/2p\ne1/2p=1/2. Hence

Anσ≅⨁m=0nM(nm).A_n^\sigma\cong\bigoplus_{m=0}^nM_{\binom nm}.Anσ​≅m=0⨁n​M(mn​)​.

These algebras increase. Equivariance gives En(x)∈AnσE_n(x)\in A_n^\sigmaEn​(x)∈Anσ​ for every x∈Nx\in Nx∈N, and Exercise 2 gives strong* convergence to xxx. Their strong closure is therefore NNN, proving AFD without a classification or named-factor identification.

Exercise 7. Suppose only some integer spectral degrees occurred. Identify the step of Theorem 4.2 that would fail.

Solution. The factorial corner step still makes a central element diagonal with scalar blocks qnzqn=cnqnq_nzq_n=c_nq_nqn​zqn​=cn​qn​. To compare two scalars, however, one needs an actual nonzero block qnπ(x)qmq_n\pi(x)q_mqn​π(x)qm​. A degree-kkk coefficient sends Fourier degree mmm to m−km-km−k, so the proof's direct comparison of arbitrary n,mn,mn,m requires a nonzero degree k=m−nk=m-nk=m−n.

With a restricted degree set, these direct blocks may be absent. Make a graph with vertices Z\mathbb ZZ, joining n,mn,mn,m whenever such a block is nonzero. Commutation gives cn=cmc_n=c_mcn​=cm​ on every edge and therefore along each finite path. It does not compare different connected components. Thus missing degrees do not automatically prove nonfactoriality; sufficient chains could still connect the indices. What fails is the argument that every pair has the direct nonzero block (15). If the indices split into components, distinct scalar values on them are no longer excluded by that argument. For a trivial action only degree zero occurs, and the Fourier projections themselves give central blocks. This also demonstrates why factoriality of the corners alone cannot replace the degree-connection step.

Exercise 12. A single matrix algebra M2M_2M2​ with density ρ\rhoρ has the same modular-action period PPP. Why cannot Theorem 6.1 assign it the same type III subtype?

Solution. Every projection in M2M_2M2​ is finite, and the normalized matrix trace is a faithful normal finite trace. This algebra is the type I factor M2M_2M2​, so it fails both the infinite-dimensional and type III hypotheses of Theorem 6.1.

One can see the invariant obstruction directly. For its trace, the closed GNS involution has modular operator 111, so the intersection over all faithful normal semifinite weights is contained in {1}\{1\}{1}, excluding the proposed type III invariant. Here is the finite-dimensional justification. By GW1–4, the finite left ideal is a linear ultraweakly dense subspace. On a finite matrix algebra the matrix-entry coefficients give the ultraweak topology, and every linear subspace is closed in this finite-dimensional topology. Density therefore makes the finite left ideal the whole algebra. In particular the identity has finite weight, and monotonicity gives finite weight to every rank-one projection. For completeness, semifiniteness makes each rank-one projection eee have finite weight: a nonzero finite-weight positive element below eee is cecece, c>0c>0c>0. Adding the two orthogonal rank-one projections gives finite weight at 111. The weight is therefore a bounded positive matrix functional, represented by a positive invertible density by faithfulness. In its diagonal Hilbert–Schmidt model the modular operator fixes the diagonal matrix vectors. Thus 111 occurs for every faithful normal semifinite weight and S(M2)={1}S(M_2)=\{1\}S(M2​)={1}.

For the nontracial state with density ρ\rhoρ, its fixed algebra is the two-dimensional diagonal algebra, which is not a factor. The modular operator on the four-dimensional Hilbert–Schmidt space has eigenvalues 1,1,r,r−11,1,r,r^{-1}1,1,r,r−1, and the only action degrees are 0,±10,\pm10,±1. Consequently Theorem 3.2's factorial-centralizer step fails, and the direct block of Theorem 4.2 is absent whenever ∣m−n∣≥2|m-n|\ge2∣m−n∣≥2. The infinite-coordinate permutation ergodicity used in Theorem 3.2 has no counterpart in this single-mode calculation. At the half-state the centralizer is instead all of M2M_2M2​, but the state is tracial and still supplies no type III conclusion. A modular-action period is a property of the chosen state; the infinite product supplies the nonsemifiniteness, factorial centralizer and complete degree structure used in the original core proof.

8. Projection comparison and the finite-factor alternative

This gives the projection argument needed at the end of Theorem 3.2. Let M⊆B(H)M\subseteq B(H)M⊆B(H) be a unital strongly closed *-algebra, with HHH arbitrary. Sections 8.1–8.9 assume no separability, countable decomposition, trace, faithful state, modular action or factor type. Projection sums indexed by arbitrary sets mean nets of finite subsums.

The support, comparison and minimal-projection methods are compared with Anantharaman and Popa, An introduction to II₁ factors, Proposition 2.2.4, Theorem 2.4.1, Proposition 2.4.2, Lemmas 2.4.6–2.4.7, Theorem 2.4.8, Corollary 2.4.9, and Proposition 2.4.13, printed pp.32–34 and 36–39 (PDF pp.38–40 and 42–45). Corollary 2.4.14, printed p.40/PDF p.46, states the finite tracial alternative. The proof below supplies central-support details, arbitrary orthogonal sums, scalar minimal corners and full matrix-unit surjectivity. Positive roots and supports are constructed directly, so the general continuous or Borel spectral calculus is not an input.

8.1. The elementary operator facts used below

The baseline is complex Hilbert-space completeness, scalar arithmetic and convergent power series, adjoints of bounded operators, and Zorn's lemma (the usual choice principle). The following elementary facts make explicit the analytic prerequisites of the subsequent arguments.

The underlying Cauchy–Schwarz estimate, adjoints, completeness of B(H)B(H)B(H), finite Gram–Schmidt and tensor positivity/completion are supplied in Infinite tensor products and their reference states, Sections 10.1–10.4. Only those concrete Hilbert/operator constructions are used here.

For a bounded self-adjoint operator aaa,

∥a∥=sup⁡∥ξ∥≤1∣⟨ξ,aξ⟩∣.\|a\|=\sup_{\|\xi\|\le1}|\langle\xi,a\xi\rangle|.∥a∥=∥ξ∥≤1sup​∣⟨ξ,aξ⟩∣.

Indeed, let the supremum on the right be mmm. For unit vectors ξ,η\xi,\etaξ,η, real polarization and the parallelogram identity give

∣Re⁡⟨η,aξ⟩∣≤m4(∥ξ+η∥2+∥ξ−η∥2)=m.|\operatorname{Re}\langle\eta,a\xi\rangle| \le\tfrac m4(\|\xi+\eta\|^2+\|\xi-\eta\|^2)=m.∣Re⟨η,aξ⟩∣≤4m​(∥ξ+η∥2+∥ξ−η∥2)=m.

A positive form satisfies Cauchy--Schwarz by applying its nonnegativity to ξ+tη\xi+t\etaξ+tη and minimizing in t∈Ct\in\mathbb Ct∈C. Consequently ⟨ξ,aξ⟩=0\langle\xi,a\xi\rangle=0⟨ξ,aξ⟩=0 for a≥0a\ge0a≥0 implies aξ=0a\xi=0aξ=0.

Every closed subspace L⊆HL\subseteq HL⊆H has an orthogonal projection. For completeness, a sequence approaching the infimum distance from ξ\xiξ to LLL is Cauchy by the parallelogram identity applied to its two members and their midpoint. Completeness and closedness give a minimizing vector η∈L\eta\in Lη∈L. Minimality applied to η+tz\eta+tzη+tz, for z∈Lz\in Lz∈L and t∈Ct\in\mathbb Ct∈C, gives ξ−η⊥L\xi-\eta\perp Lξ−η⊥L. The resulting decomposition H=L⊕L⊥H=L\oplus L^\perpH=L⊕L⊥ is unique, linear, and its projection has norm at most one. In particular

ran⁡a‾=(ker⁡a∗)⊥,\overline{\operatorname{ran} a}=(\ker a^*)^\perp,rana=(kera∗)⊥,

because a vector is orthogonal to the range exactly when its image under a∗a^*a∗ is zero.

Norm limits of elements of MMM belong to MMM, since norm convergence implies strong convergence. Uniformly bounded strong limits multiply when both factors converge strongly: for ai→aa_i\to aai​→a, bi→bb_i\to bbi​→b,

∥(aibi−ab)ξ∥≤∥ai∥ ∥(bi−b)ξ∥+∥(ai−a)bξ∥.\|(a_i b_i-ab)\xi\| \le\|a_i\|\,\|(b_i-b)\xi\|+\|(a_i-a)b\xi\|.∥(ai​bi​−ab)ξ∥≤∥ai​∥∥(bi​−b)ξ∥+∥(ai​−a)bξ∥.

We will use this only for explicitly bounded nets. An adjoint limit will always be proved separately, rather than inferred from strong convergence alone.

The bounded monotone completeness used to describe normality at Section 8.9 also has a Hilbert-space proof. The Hilbert Riesz representation needed here follows from the projection argument above: the kernel of a nonzero bounded linear functional is a closed subspace of codimension one; projecting any vector outside the kernel onto its orthogonal complement yields a nonzero vector spanning that complement, and the functional is a scalar multiple of the inner product against it. Applying this separately to each variable identifies a bounded sesquilinear form with a unique bounded operator. This section gives full proofs of Lemma 2.1, Lemma 2.2 and Theorem 3.2 in Constant CAR states and the periodic core. The actual inputs are the complete concrete Hilbert/operator proofs in ITP10.1–10.6, the whole faithful identical-product construction, Tomita graph and coordinate action in ITP11.1–11.8, the completed pointed normal bridge in CAR15, and the whole modular-graph transport in current CAR17.2–17.3/17.6. The expectations, diagonal and actual finite permutation unitaries are respectively W∗En(W ⋅ W∗)WW^*E_n(W\,\cdot\,W^*)WW∗En​(W⋅W∗)W, W∗DWW^*DWW∗DW, and W∗vπWW^*v_\pi WW∗vπ​W. Strong* convergence transports on every vector. Therefore original Lemma2.1, Lemma2.2 and Theorem3.2 refer to the whole actual completed CAR/product representation, not merely an agreement of local moments.

The positive/projection comparison is Claire Anantharaman and Sorin Popa, An introduction to II1 factors, exact freely accessible 338-page draft, SHA-256 09e63a8b2060ed9f7569c4898a4ead0581e34b8160524c4952702731f131d52f. The relevant comparisons are Proposition 2.2.4, Theorem 2.4.1, Proposition 2.4.2, Lemmas 2.4.6–2.4.7, Theorem 2.4.8, Corollary 2.4.9, Proposition 2.4.13 and Corollary 2.4.14, printed pp.32–40. The scalar-corner and surjectivity arguments needed here are given explicitly above; the application does not require the draft's spectral or Kaplansky arguments. The broader projection-comparison theorem is available as a fully proved local provider, but this application needs only the contact/minimal-corner/finite matrix branch.

The non-half hypothesis is retained throughout this centralizer proof, although some local slice and trace arguments also apply at half. At p=0,1p=0,1p=0,1, invertibility, separating cyclicity and positive occupation weights used here fail. A finite one-particle space has no unbounded supply of new coordinates or arbitrarily fine infinite occupation partitions, so this proof gives no finite-dimensional centralizer conclusion. Nonidentical densities do not generally give permutation unitaries in the fixed algebra; nonseparable or arbitrary-index products are outside this countable target.

The exact measure-space version of original Lemma3.1 and the identification in original (10) remain separate. This proof does not construct the Bernoulli probability measure, prove the measure/cylinder completion, or infer the function lemma merely from the operator argument. It completely supplies the operator route to Theorem3.2 without them. General modular centralizer identities, arbitrary-factor trace existence, product semifiniteness criteria, type III subtype, compact/real crossed products, scalar Fourier or measurable-phase theorems, continuous-core trace/center/flow, and the remaining course prerequisites lie outside this section.

The circle crossing, vector slices and all-weight spectrum calculation use three closure facts and one scalar normalization. Their complete earlier constructions are CF1–10, CP01–06, scalar integration SC, and the disk and quarter-phase proof, Section 8.4.

Bibliographic scope

Jan Dereziński, Introduction to representations of the canonical commutation and anticommutation relations, arXiv:math-ph/0511030v2, Theorem 43(10), printed/PDF p.48, states the constant-covariance type IIIλ\mathrm{III}_\lambdaIIIλ​ result; it does not supply a complete classification proof.

The main calculations include the complete normal occupation-diagonal identification, finite-density centralizer identity, operator permutation proof, direct exclusion of finite projections, coefficient-domain modular spectrum, Fourier corners, period-circle factor, lattice transform and vector-slice center computation. The exact completed CAR bridge, finite-factor trace and weighted modular graphs are the supplied full proofs in Infinite tensor products and Fermions, Fock and quasi-free factors. Periodic corner spectra from factor contact supplies the interval filters and two nonzero support contacts. The full finite-ideal and every-weight comparison in MG-0–3, with its balanced-weight and fixed-corner graph proofs, supplies the lower bound on the modular intersection; the explicitly computed product spectrum supplies the upper bound. Their deeper prerequisites retain their own stated scopes. Sections 8–11 give the projection, expectation and operator-centralizer arguments, the coefficient-predual and ultraweak-density arguments, and the scalar circle normalization, with the hypotheses for each argument stated in place. The infinite-dimensional and type III hypotheses remain essential, as Exercise 12 verifies.

Alain Connes, Une classification des facteurs de type III, Annales scientifiques de l’École Normale Supérieure 6 (1973), 133–252, gives the action-spectrum definition on printed p.170, the full fixed-corner and equivalence development in Section 2.2 on pp.174–177, and the modular intersection development on pp.190–192. The explicit periodic filters and support witnesses are supplied in PP01–PP04, and the full all-weight calculation used here is specified in Section 6. The source's broader action-realization prerequisites are not imported by citation. Its introduction to Part IV on printed p.213 gives the type notation used for the closed discrete invariant. Source credit does not replace the all-weight proof.

The exact prerequisite proof versions used in the weight comparison are collected in the weight foundations. The selected arguments carry their source attribution and applicable licence notices.
